tracks.name: Cybersecurity
tracks.desc: A full, ethical journey from zero to job-ready cybersecurity: the CIA triad, networking, passwords and hashing, ciphers (Caesar, XOR), public-key crypto and HTTPS, how attacks work and how to stop them, web security, secure coding, blue-team defence and monitoring, and how to build an ethical-hacking career. Concepts and defence only — never real attack tooling.
outcomes: Explain and apply the CIA triad
Recognise and defend against real attacks
Prevent web vulnerabilities in your own code
Defend, monitor and respond as a blue team
Start an ethical-hacking career the legal way

lessons.title: What cybersecurity is: the CIA triad
lessons.content:
Protecting information from harm

Cybersecurity is keeping data and systems safe from people who shouldn't reach them. Everything in the field maps to three goals — the CIA triad:

  • Confidentiality — only the right people can read the data (encryption, passwords, access control).
  • Integrity — the data hasn't been secretly changed (hashing, checksums, signatures).
  • Availability — the system is up when you need it (backups, defending against overload).

Attackers vs defenders

People who defend systems are the blue team; people who test them (with permission) to find weaknesses are the red team / ethical hackers. This whole course is about defending, and about hacking only with permission — attacking systems you don't own is a crime.

Golden rule of ethics: never test, probe or attack a system you do not own or have written permission to test. Curiosity is good; consent is mandatory.

exercises.q: A hacker reads private messages they shouldn't. Which of the CIA triad is broken? Print exactly: Confidentiality
exercises.starter: # which goal is broken when private data is read?
exercises.hint: Reading data you shouldn't breaks confidentiality.

exercises.q: Someone secretly edits a bank record. Which goal is broken? Print exactly: Integrity
A website is knocked offline so no one can use it. Which goal is broken? Print exactly: Availability

lessons.title: How data travels: the internet, safely
lessons.content:
Addresses, names and ports

Every device online has an IP address (like a street address). DNS turns a name like example.com into that address. Programs talk through numbered ports — e.g. web traffic uses port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS).

HTTP vs HTTPS

HTTP sends data in the clear — anyone in between can read it. HTTPS wraps it in TLS encryption, so it stays private and can't be tampered with. The padlock in your browser means HTTPS. Never type a password into a plain http:// page.

https://shop.example.com:443/cart
  |         |            |    |
scheme     host        port  path

exercises.q: Print the standard port for HTTPS (secure web). It is 443.
From the URL, print the host part. The URL is 'https://shop.example.com/cart'.
exercises.starter:
url = 'https://shop.example.com/cart'
# get the host between :// and the next /
exercises.hint: Split off 'https://', then take up to the first '/'.

exercises.q: A page starts with 'http://'. Is it safe to enter a password? Print 'unsafe' if it is plain http.
exercises.starter:
url = 'http://login.example.com'
# http (no s) is not encrypted
exercises.hint: If it starts with http:// (not https://) it's unsafe.

lessons.title: Passwords done right
lessons.content:
Why length beats complexity

A short "clever" password like P@ss1 is weak; a long passphrase like correct-horse-battery-staple is far stronger because there are vastly more possibilities to guess. Length is the biggest factor.

Never store passwords as plain text

Systems must never keep your actual password. They store a hash (a scrambled, one-way fingerprint) with a random salt so two people with the same password get different stored values. When you log in, they hash what you typed and compare. This course's own backend uses bcrypt for exactly this.

If a website can email you your original password, they're storing it unsafely — a red flag.

exercises.q: Write a simple strength check: a password is 'strong' if it is at least 12 characters. Test 'correct-horse-battery' and print strong or weak.
Test the password 'P@ss1' with the same rule (>=12 chars). Print strong or weak.
Check a password against a tiny 'common passwords' list. If 'password123' is in the banned list, print 'banned'.
exercises.solution:
banned=['123456','password','password123','qwerty']
pw='password123'
print('banned' if pw in banned else 'ok')

lessons.title: Your first cipher: Caesar
lessons.content:
Shifting letters to hide a message

The Caesar cipher shifts every letter forward by a fixed number. Shift 3: A→D, B→E, ... This is easy to break (only 25 shifts to try) but it teaches the core idea of encryption: a reversible transformation controlled by a key.

plain:  H E L L O
shift+3
cipher: K H O O R

To decrypt, shift back by the same amount. In Python, ord('A') gives a letter's number and chr() turns a number back into a letter.

exercises.q: Shift the single uppercase letter 'A' forward by 3 using ord/chr. Print the result (D).
Encrypt the word 'HELLO' with a Caesar shift of 3. Print the cipher text (KHOOR).
exercises.starter:
word = 'HELLO'
shift = 3
out = ''
# shift each letter, build out
exercises.solution:
word='HELLO'; shift=3; out=''
for c in word:
    out+=chr((ord(c)-65+shift)%26+65)
print(out)

exercises.q: Decrypt 'KHOOR' back with a shift of 3 (shift the other way). Print HELLO.
exercises.starter:
word = 'KHOOR'
shift = 3
out = ''
# subtract the shift
exercises.solution:
word='KHOOR'; shift=3; out=''
for c in word:
    out+=chr((ord(c)-65-shift)%26+65)
print(out)

lessons.title: XOR and symmetric encryption
lessons.content:
One key to lock and unlock

Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt. A simple example is XOR: combine each byte of the message with a key byte. XOR has a magic property — doing it twice with the same key gives you back the original.

5 XOR 3 = 6      (encrypt)
6 XOR 3 = 5      (decrypt — back to the start!)

Real symmetric ciphers like AES are far stronger, but they rest on this same "shared secret key" idea. The hard part in real life is sharing the key safely — which is what public-key crypto (next lessons) solves.

exercises.q: Compute 5 XOR 3 in Python (the ^ operator). Print it.
XOR is reversible. Take 6 (the cipher) XOR 3 (the key) and print it — you should get the original 5.
Encrypt the number list [72, 73] by XOR-ing each with key 10, then print the encrypted list.
exercises.starter:
msg = [72, 73]
key = 10
# xor each with key
exercises.solution:
msg=[72,73]; key=10
print([m ^ key for m in msg])

lessons.title: Hashing and integrity
lessons.content:
A one-way fingerprint

A hash turns any data into a fixed-size fingerprint. It's one-way: you can't get the data back from the hash. Change one character of the input and the hash changes completely. That makes hashes perfect for two jobs:

  • Integrity — download a file, hash it, compare to the published hash. If they match, the file wasn't tampered with.
  • Password storage — store the hash, never the password.

Hashing is not encryption. Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is deliberately not reversible.

exercises.q: A tiny 'checksum' hash: add up the character codes of 'HI' (H=72, I=73) and print the total.
exercises.starter:
s = 'HI'
# sum of ord() of each character
exercises.solution:
s='HI'
print(sum(ord(c) for c in s))

exercises.q: Show that changing one letter changes the checksum: print the checksum of 'HJ' (H=72, J=74).
exercises.solution:
s='HJ'
print(sum(ord(c) for c in s))

exercises.q: Integrity check: the published checksum is 145. Our file's checksum is 145. Print 'ok' if they match, else 'tampered'.
exercises.solution:
published=145; file_sum=145
print('ok' if published==file_sum else 'tampered')

lessons.title: Public-key cryptography & HTTPS
lessons.content:
Two keys: one public, one private

Asymmetric crypto uses a pair of keys. Anything locked with your public key can only be unlocked with your private key (which you never share). This solves the "how do we agree a secret over the open internet?" problem.

  • Encrypt with public key → only the private-key holder can read it.
  • Sign with private key → anyone can verify it with your public key (proves it's really you).

What HTTPS actually does

When you visit an https:// site, your browser and the server use public-key crypto to agree on a temporary shared key, check the site's certificate (proving it's the real site), then switch to fast symmetric encryption for the rest. That's the padlock.

exercises.q: The core of RSA is modular arithmetic. Compute (7 ** 3) % 33 in Python and print it.
Python has a built-in for modular exponentiation: pow(base, exp, mod). Print pow(7, 3, 33).
A certificate is valid if today (day 100) is before its expiry (day 365). Print 'valid' or 'expired'.
exercises.solution:
today=100; expiry=365
print('valid' if today<expiry else 'expired')

lessons.title: How attacks work — so you can stop them
lessons.content:
Know the enemy (to defend)

Most breaches don't use movie-style hacking — they use these:

  • Phishing — a fake email/message tricking you into a password or a bad link. The #1 way real breaches start.
  • Social engineering — manipulating a person ("IT here, I need your password").
  • Malware — malicious software (viruses, ransomware, spyware) run by mistake.
  • Brute force — trying millions of passwords. Long passwords + rate limits + lockouts defeat it.

Spotting phishing

Warning signs: urgency ("act now!"), a mismatched sender address, a link whose real destination differs from its text, unexpected attachments, and requests for passwords or payment. When unsure, go to the site directly instead of clicking.

We teach how attacks work only to defend against them. Building or sending real malware or phishing is illegal and off-limits.

exercises.q: A brute-force attacker tries 1000 passwords per second. A lockout triggers after 5 tries. Print how many tries the attacker actually gets (5).
exercises.starter:
lockout_after = 5
# the attacker is stopped at the lockout

exercises.q: Flag a phishing sign: the email demands you 'verify your password now'. If the text contains 'password', print 'phishing'.
exercises.starter:
email = 'Urgent: verify your password now'
# a request for your password is a red flag
exercises.solution:
email='Urgent: verify your password now'
print('phishing' if 'password' in email.lower() else 'ok')

exercises.q: Check a link: the visible text says 'bank.com' but the real URL is 'bank-secure.ru'. If they don't match, print 'suspicious'.
exercises.solution:
text='bank.com'; real='bank-secure.ru'
print('suspicious' if text!=real else 'ok')

lessons.title: Web security: injection & XSS (and how to prevent them)
lessons.content:
Never trust user input

Most web vulnerabilities come from mixing untrusted input with code or HTML.

SQL injection

If you build a query by gluing strings together, an attacker can inject SQL. The fix is parameterized queries — the database treats input as data, never as code.

# WRONG — vulnerable
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"

# RIGHT — parameterized
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))

Cross-site scripting (XSS)

If you put user text straight into a page, they can inject a <script>. The fix is to escape output — turn < into < so it shows as text, not code.

The lesson everywhere: validate input, and escape/parameterize output. This app does both.

exercises.q: Escape a dangerous character: replace '<' with '<' in the string "<script>". Print the safe version.
Basic input validation: a username should be letters/numbers only. Print 'valid' if 'Ravi42' is alphanumeric, else 'invalid'.
Reject a suspicious input: does "a' OR '1'='1" contain a single quote? If yes print 'reject'.
exercises.starter:
inp = "a' OR '1'='1"
# a quote in a name is suspicious
exercises.solution:
inp="a' OR '1'='1"
print('reject' if "'" in inp else 'allow')

lessons.title: Secure coding & handling secrets
lessons.content:
Habits that prevent most bugs

  • Validate all input — assume anything from a user or the network is hostile.
  • Least privilege — give every account and program the minimum access it needs.
  • Never hard-code secrets — keep API keys and passwords in environment variables, never in code or a public repo (this app's keys live in Railway variables, not the code).
  • Keep dependencies updated — most breaches exploit known bugs in out-of-date libraries.
  • Fail safely — on error, deny access; never reveal stack traces or secrets to users.

exercises.q: A secret key should come from the environment, not the code. If the variable API_KEY is empty, print 'missing key' (never use a default secret).
exercises.solution:
API_KEY=''
print('missing key' if not API_KEY else 'ok')

exercises.q: Least privilege: a 'guest' role should NOT be able to delete. Print 'denied' when role is 'guest' and action is 'delete'.
exercises.solution:
role='guest'; action='delete'
print('denied' if (role=='guest' and action=='delete') else 'allowed')

exercises.q: Validate age input is a number before using it. If '25' is all digits, print the age plus 1 (26).

lessons.title: Defence & monitoring (Blue Team)
lessons.content:
You can't stop what you can't see

Defenders watch systems constantly. Key ideas:

  • Logging — record logins, errors and important actions. Logs are how you spot and reconstruct an attack.
  • IDS / SIEM — tools that watch logs and network traffic for suspicious patterns and raise alerts.
  • Rate limiting & lockouts — stop brute force by capping attempts.
  • Backups — the answer to ransomware is a clean, tested backup.

Incident response (the calm checklist)

Prepare → Detect → Contain → Eradicate → Recover → Learn. Panicking or hiding a breach makes it worse; a rehearsed plan makes it survivable.

exercises.q: Count failed logins in a log to spot an attack. Given the list, print how many are 'FAIL'.
Raise an alert if failed logins exceed 4. There were 6. Print 'ALERT' or 'quiet'.
exercises.solution:
fails=6; threshold=4
print('ALERT' if fails>threshold else 'quiet')

exercises.q: Incident response order: print the FIRST step of the checklist. Print exactly: Prepare

lessons.title: Ethical hacking & a cybersecurity career
lessons.content:
Hacking — the legal, paid kind

Penetration testers and bug-bounty hunters break into systems with permission to find weaknesses before criminals do. It is one of the best-paid, most in-demand areas in tech, and it is global and remote-friendly.

Roles

  • SOC analyst / Blue team — monitor and defend (great first job).
  • Penetration tester / Red team — authorised attacking to find holes.
  • Security engineer — build defences into products.
  • GRC / compliance — policies, risk, audits (less coding).

How to get in

Learn the fundamentals (this track), practise legally on sites built for it — TryHackMe, Hack The Box, PortSwigger Web Security Academy, OverTheWire — and aim for a certificate like CompTIA Security+ (entry), then CEH or OSCP (hands-on). Build a habit of writing up what you learn.

The line that defines your career: only ever test systems you own or are explicitly authorised to test. Unauthorised access is a serious crime — ethics is the whole job.

exercises.q: The one rule of ethical hacking: you must have this before testing a system. Print exactly: permission
exercises.starter: # what must you always have first?

exercises.q: A good entry-level certificate for cybersecurity. Print exactly: Security+
